patch.value: Workspace federation: cross-workspace references, remote dependency resolution, and aggregated bounded context without a central server

The federation story is filed as an organizational need with no implementation owner. It is the natural scale boundary: a single workspace scales by index and packing work already underway, but an organization with many repositories has many workspaces, and the questions that matter cross them — what blocks this item lives in another repository's tracker, what is the aggregate state of a programme spanning eight repositories, which agent in which workspace holds the claim on the shared dependency. Design this the way the rest of pm is designed: no central server, no live coupling, git-native. A workspace declares peers by repository coordinate; cross-workspace references are first-class identifiers that resolve through a locally cached, verifiable snapshot of the peer's public projection; aggregation is a read-side fold over those snapshots with explicit staleness reporting, never a distributed transaction. Writes stay strictly local — a federated reference can be observed and depended upon but never mutated remotely — which keeps the immutability and merge guarantees intact and makes the whole feature safe to adopt incrementally. Cross-workspace cycles, unreachable peers, and stale snapshots must be reported as facts in the output rather than treated as errors, because in a federation partial knowledge is the normal state.

A workspace declares peers by repository coordinate, and cross-workspace references are first-class identifiers distinguishable from local ones in every projection; Peer state is a locally cached, integrity-verified snapshot of the peer's public projection, and every read reports the snapshot's age; Aggregation across peers is a bounded read-side fold that honors the token budget and reports partial results with named missing peers rather than failing; Writes to a peer workspace are impossible through federation, asserted by a test that attempts every mutation path against a federated reference; A cross-workspace dependency cycle is detected and reported as a fact with the participating workspaces named, never as a crash or a silent drop; An unreachable peer degrades to last-known state with explicit staleness, and a workspace with no peers behaves exactly as it does today, proven by snapshot; Federated identifiers survive merge, history replay, and format migration with the same guarantees as local identifiers
Context assembly answers questions that span repositories without any workspace giving up local authority
The largest deployments are inherently multi-repository; without federation the product's ceiling is one repository regardless of how well a single workspace scales
Introduces the first identifiers that point outside a workspace; the design must keep write authority local or the immutability and merge guarantees weaken
An organization runs one tracker per repository and still gets programme-level context, dependency resolution, and aggregation

value.author: harness:codex
value.text: Federation design without a mandatory central server: use globally scoped workspace identities plus local item IDs, signed workspace manifests, explicit remote relationship types, versioned schema/capability negotiation, and trust policies that distinguish authoritative, cached, unavailable, stale, and unverified data. Resolve context through bounded parallel fan-out, per-remote budgets/deadlines, local cache and freshness receipts, top-k score calibration, deterministic partial-result merging, and continuation tokens that preserve each remote cursor. Support offline-first operation and partial replication by exchanging content-addressed event segments, Merkle summaries, causal watermarks/vector summaries, and compensating events; never rewrite a remote history or collapse an unresolved cross-workspace conflict. Security boundaries include allowlisted fields, credential isolation, provenance/attestation verification, hostile payload limits, recursion/cycle budgets, and tenant-safe redaction. Validate on one-item ephemeral projects, multi-decade archives, million-item shards, network partitions, schema skew, repository moves, remote deletion, resurrection, and thousand-agent fan-in. Publish completeness, staleness, trust, omission, latency, token, and unresolved-reference receipts so an agent can distinguish a complete answer from the best available partial answer.
